Mr. Lynch's article indicates that a particular speech which the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George made at a meeting of the Dominion Marine Association was in effect a cream puff speech which contained nothing of substance. The speech made by the minister the other evening at that meeting in Montreal contained one of the most important declarations regarding the field of shipping and the shipping industry to be made in Canada. In that speech the minister declared that for the first time in Canada's history, even though the authority has been in the Canada Shipping Act probably since confederation, the government is going to establish manning scales for ships plying the lakes, and will concentrate in the first instance on departmental ships and large modern lakers used by private industry.
This declaration will serve the purpose of saving the lives of many Canadian sailors and
will prevent a great deal of damage to the industry itself.
I will not conclude my question of privilege by moving a motion, but if I were to do so I would do so by paraphrasing the words of Mr. Lynch and say "Please, Charlie baby, from now on read all the words of the speeches". [DOT] (11:10 a.m.)

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. Yesterday I drew his attention to a Washington dispatch which quoted Ross Flannigan, chairman of a Quaker action group, alleging that Air Canada had refused to accept shipments of medical supplies which the Quakers wanted to send to North Viet Nam. I asked the minister at that time if he would make inquiries of Air Canada and find out whether these allegations were correct.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. W. Pickersgill (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: TABLING OF LIST OF MEMBERS OF EXPORT ADVISORY COUNCIL
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STEPS BY U.S. TO WITHHOLD SUPPLIES FROM NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had inquiries made of Air Canada and was informed that they had received a request for free or reduced rate transportation for medical supplies to be shipped by Air Canada to Moscow destined for North Viet Nam.
Under the IATA regulations, resolution 200, paragraph 2c, member air lines are allowed to send "any person or supplies to provide relief in case of general epidemic, disaster or other calamitous visitation but not transportation to or from zones of military operation". Air Canada as a common carrier cannot refuse and has not refused to accept revenue shipments of this nature, but it is prohibited from providing free or reduced transportation under the IATA regulations. The Russian air line Aeroflot is not a member of IATA and therefore I assume would not be limited in the same way.

maintopic: TABLING OF LIST OF MEMBERS OF EXPORT ADVISORY COUNCIL
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS

speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Is my understanding of what the minister said correct, that the only reason for refusing to handle these medical supplies was the request that they be shipped either free or at a reduced rate, and that if the Quakers were willing to pay the regular rate Air Canada would be willing to carry these supplies?

Mr. Speaker, yesterday I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether his attention had been drawn to a report in the Toronto Star in which it was alleged that Mr. Somer-field, chief counsel of the treasury department, foreign assets control, of the United States has said that his department has forbidden Canadian subsidiaries of United States pharmaceutical organizations to sell anything to the Quakers for shipment to North Viet Nam. The minister said that he had not seen the report, and I will quote him from page 11976 of yesterday's Hansard:
I have not seen the report, Mr. Speaker. When I do see it I will judge what action, if any, should be taken.
May I ask the minister now whether he has seen the report and what action, if any, he intends to take.

speakeroldname: Hon. Roberi Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: TABLING OF LIST OF MEMBERS OF EXPORT ADVISORY COUNCIL
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STEPS BY U.S. TO WITHHOLD SUPPLIES FROM NORTH VIET NAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have seen the report, in fact I have a copy of it before me now. I got in touch at once with our embassy in Washington through the regular channels. The embassy then was in touch with the United States government, and has been advised that neither the department of state nor the department of treasury of the United States government has issued any special directives to United States drug companies to instruct their subsidiary companies in Canada to refuse to sell medical supplies for transmission to North Viet Nam. As the hon. member knows, in the United States there are foreign assets control regulations and North Viet Nam is one of the prohibited areas. However, there have been no recent developments with respect to trading by Canadian companies, and the United States is well aware of our attitude in this regard. It is understood that the Canadian Friends' Service Committee finds no difficulty in obtaining from Canadian companies the medical supplies which it needs.

When the committee rose last evening, new section 336 of clause 53 of the bill, with an amendment by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, was under consideration. The proposed amendment is as follows:
That a new subsection be added as subsection (2| of section 336 as follows:
A shipper of goods in respect of which the rates in effect on the 1st day of January, 1965, were class and commodity rates subject to the Freight Rates Reduction Act, shall be deemed to have no alternative, effective and competitive service by a common carrier other than a rail carrier or carriers or combination of rail carriers.

January 20, 1967

speechtext:
I was speaking when the time came tor adjournment last night, and I should like now to continue my remarks and summarize what I believe the effect ot this amendment would be.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
In order to benefit from this particular clause one must have no alternative effective competition. He then must apply to this board and assert and prove that he is in a captive position. I should like to make this very clear. This is what caused the minister to be in difficulty yesterday. A person cannot just apply in order to be classed as a captive shipper. His rate may be 300 per cent above the variable cost so he would very much benefit if his rate was governed by this particular clause; but he cannot just apply, say that he wishes to become a captive shipper, and all of a sudden become one. He must assert and prove that he is in a captive position. In order to prove this he must declare that 100 per cent of his commodity will move by a given railway.
The effect this amendment has on this clause is that it broadens the definition of captive shipper and broadens the definition of captive locality. I think it is a very worth while amendment because of the phrase "alternative effective competition". In effect the clause says "Let us accept everybody who had to ship goods under class and non-competitive rates when the Freight Rates Reduction Act came in; let us accept them as being in a captive position, and let us accept them as being captive shippers". This then would allow these people and these areas to apply for and receive the maximum formula, if it would benefit them.
Last evening the minister said he thought this maximum formula clause would benefit very few. He said in effect that it is of very little benefit. If the clause were broadened as suggested by this amendment a greater degree of protection would be given to the western parts of Canada and the maritime region. I say this because if one goes back to the 196465 committee reports at page 968 it will be found from the waybill analysis which is set out there that, apart from grain moving under Crowsnest pass rates, nearly 60 per cent of all the freight moving into and out of western Canada moves under class and non-competitive rates. The same is true in respect of the maritime area.
From a study of the same report one can ascertain that from eastern to western Canada 44.4 per cent of the freight moves under class
[The Chairman ]
and non-competitive rates which were frozen under the Freight Rates Reduction Act. Without this broadening amendment this clause in the bill has the effect of throwing to the wolves the freight rates of western Canada and the maritimes. It has the effect of saying that we now think there is competition out there but it has not been proven.
The government has been convinced by the railways. This is part of the agreement the minister made with the C.P.R., and which he read out on January 12. Not too long ago, in outlining this point, the minister mentioned that he felt the C.P.R. now should pay taxes on various property out there. This is part of the agreement the minister made. He said we are not worried about western Canada and the maritimes any more. He said we accept the fact that there is competition there. There is not absolute competition there, because they still are shipping goods under non-competitive rates.
If this amendment is not accepted the effect will be that freight rates will go up 50 per cent within five years on goods moving into and out of western Canada and on goods moving into and out of the maritimes. It will even have the effect of increasing the freight rates in and around the maritimes. Some 55.8 per cent of the goods shipped on railways moving in and around the maritimes moves under class and non-competitive rates. Without this amendment to this clause those rates will go up and up because in this bill there is no protection for this area. We all know that in the period between 1948 and 1958 freight rates increased 157 per cent. If this amendment is not accepted I predict that within five years from the passage of this bill freight rates in Canada in these particular areas at least will go up by 50 per cent.
Every member in this house should be aware of the fact that transportation plays a major part in the final cost of any goods. The mining association said that transportation accounts for 50 per cent to 70 per cent of the cost in respect of the final product. We have seen in the past year the effect of inflation. With the passage of this bill we would be adding fuel to the inflationary fires. If this amendment were accepted there would be some protection. The inflationary fires still would be there, but they would be smoking rather than burning brightly. I urge the members of th's committee to consider this amendment very seriously, because it gives some protection to the areas of Canada which are still being developed, namely western Canada and the maritimes. Without this amendment
January 20, 1967

freight rates will go up and the inflationary fires will burn.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to prolong the debate in respect of this clause any longer than is absolutely necessary. I think the clause and the proposed amendment have had a fair hearing by the government side of the house. I submit that most of us are prepared to have the question put in respect of this amendment without any further delay.
I should like, however, to say two or three things in support of the amendment I have moved. I do not intend to recapitulate the argument I have made on this subject. I first articulated it on December 21, buttressed it on Tuesday of this past week, and elaborated on it further yesterday. It would be unnecessarily repetitive and redundant for me to go into it in further detail on this occasion.
The province of Manitoba has stated its case. The key to the issue is the definition of captive shipper. The hon. member for Acadia has said that the proposed amendment broadens the definition of captive shipper. At the same time he says the proposed amendment provides a definition of captive shipper which at the present time is missing from the proposed legislation. I was interested to hear the hon. member for Medicine Hat say last night that since the amendment he proposed failed it now is necessary to patch up the clause as it is written in order to make the best possible job out of a bad thing.
This is a laudable sentiment and one to which I subscribe. I submit, however, that this is the whole purpose of the amendment I have put forward. The purpose of the amendment is to patch up this part of the legislation in order to make clear and precise what the legislation is talking about when it refers to captive shippers and the difficulty in respect of the application of the maximum rate formula. That is precisely the purpose of the amendment.
The greatest weakness is the lack of a proper definition of the term "captive shipper". Expert after expert, such as the professors who were retained by the provinces of Manitoba and Alberta, when appearing before the committee on transport and communications, made the same point.
[DOT] (12 noon)
The western provinces themselves in their submission, and witness after witness who appeared before the committee, made the same
Transportation
point, that the legislation fails to define adequately a captive shipper. The minister has said, and I subscribe to his views, that competition is a vital and desirable thing. He has indicated that he and his colleagues are attempting by this legislation to provide a healthier climate for competition in western Canada. We on this side of the house subscribe to the same philosophy, but perhaps to a greater degree than the minister. I am certainly in favour of competition.
What we are arguing is that in this particular context the prairies, where the regions are disparate and scattered, so far as bulk commodity shippers are concerned, there is virtually no such thing as competition. We are not talking about an environment of competition or a competitive climate; we are talking in large part about a monopoly situation enjoyed by the railway companies.
What we are attempting to do here is build in some protection for the bulk shippers in western Canada who, in that particular region of this country and on this continent, since the beginning of our existence as a nation have been dependent on and captive to the railway companies. That is the entire purport and philosophy behind the amendment I have moved. We want competition, but at the present time in the climate of commercial enterprise and regional settlement which exists in the west there is not an adequate environment for competition. The railway companies do not have competition; they have this entire business in the palms of their hands.
Under those circumstances and in that context we say bulk commodity shippers on the prairies deserve, indeed vitally require, some protection, and we suggest that by this amendment some of that protection would be provided.
Let me refer once again to the case made by the province of Manitoba in respect of this point when it referred to the fact that during its deliberations and in its pronouncements the royal commission on a number of occasions referred to the Freight Rates Reduction Act is evidence of the determination of the parliament of Canada that the class of noncompetitive commodity shippers were shippers to whom the term "captive" could apply. Those are the shippers that the parliament of Canada determined should be relieved of the excessive burden caused by the last general freight rate increase in 1958.
We say in effect that virtually all western shippers of bulk commodity goods are captive shippers, and we suggest they should not have

January 20, 1967

to manifestly establish that fact before this commission because the Freight Rates Reduction Act of 1958 already affords them that status. We say they should be able to maintain that status and enjoy whatever benefits accrue to them.
That is the purport and intent of the amendment I propose, and I heartily endorse it to the minister and his colleagues on the government side of the house. I thank the minister for his kind attention to my argument.

Mr. Chairman, I should like very briefly to put to the minister the suggestion that even though the amendment just proposed to subsection 1 of new section 336 has been defeated, it is still not too late to make other improvements to the section so it
January 20, 1967

will be more fair in its effect and more effective. I suggest to the minister that even if he did not see fit to accept the amendment which would have given a more comprehensive definition to the term "captive shipper," that is one thing; but he should still give serious thought to the formula itself which will be applied by the commission in giving some protection to those, presumably very few, shippers who will be regarded as captive under the terms of this legislation.
Obviously, under subsection 2 of new section 336 the formula is that the commission shall set as a maximum a rate determined by taking the variable cost to the railways and adding 150 per cent to that variable cost. The rate shall be determined in this way. It was aptly demonstrated yesterday by other speakers and myself that it is very possible, in fact likely, that the railways, in the majority of cases where they are hauling commodities shipped by captive shippers, will be enjoying a mark-up in the order of 300 per cent and 400 per cent. I say this because the maximum rate formula, based as it is on variable cost plus 150 per cent and determined from a standard of a 30,000 pounds carload lot, will mean that in instances where the haulage is in carload lots of 70,000 pounds, 80,000 pounds,
90,000	pounds, 100,000 pounds or heavier, the mark-up will in fact be 300 per cent or 400 per cent.
In no case these days do the railways haul commodities in full carload lots of a weight less than 60,000 pounds or 70,000 pounds. When we look at the table given to the committee by the Manitoba council, and by Professors Williams and Borts, we find that the mark-up of the railways when they are hauling, under this formula, 70,000 pounds or 80,060 pounds carload lots is, as I said and I repeat again and again, in the order of 300 per cent, 400 per cent or even more. To have a maximum rate formula which allows for this kind of mark-up is simply incredible; there is no other word to describe it. It is unacceptable in every respect.
I hope the minister will see fit to accept the proposition that the formula ought to be changed so that the mark-up of the railways, when hauling goods for captive shippers, will be of an order that is deemed reasonable, just and permissible. A mark-up that is hovering around 300 per cent and 400 per cent is certainly not reasonable or just, and should not be regarded as permissible by members of this committee who are here to protect the public
Transportation
interest and the interest of shippers, particularly those shippers who are captive to the railways because of location or any other circumstance.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in order to bring this matter to a head and get the sense of members of the committee, I move:
That clause 336 subclause (2) be amended by deleting the words "150 per cent of the variable cost as the fixed rate applicable to the carriage of the goods" in lines 21 and 22 and substituting the following: "the percentage difference that total permissive earnings are to freight variable costs plus an amount computed as being the cost of capital applicable to the carriage of such goods."
Speaking to the amendment, I wish to say that if accepted it would do two things. It would remove this fictitious formula which, as I have already said, would have the effect of giving the railways the opportunity to derive unconscionable mark-ups-and I think that is the proper word-on the carriage of commodities hauled for captive shippers. In addition, it would remove what I consider to be a rather basic anomaly in this section. The basic anomaly, in my opinion, is that under the terms of this formula the railways will be able to consider the cost of capital to be a variable cost and will be able to obtain a mark-up of 150 per cent on the cost of capital. The railways are not in the banking business, and it seems to me strange that they should be able to take advantage of a formula to actually make money on money. I thought this was a function of our banking institutions and not our transportation companies.
If the cost of money is to be computed into variable cost, that is fine; but the railways should not be allowed to earn a mark-up of 150 per cent, and it may be even more, on the cost of money to them. To try and articulate this point a little more precisely I would say that the cost of the money to the railways, which is deemed to be part of their variable cost, should be treated in this way; the railways should be allowed to recover the cost of money to them, but they should not be allowed to charge a rate that will give them 150 per cent of the cost of money to them. If my amendment were accepted it would remove this anomaly.
During the committee stage and the ensuing discussion in this chamber I did not hear the minister put forward any defence of the proposition that the cost of money to the railways should be brought into this formula so the railways could receive a return of 150 per cent of the cost of money to them.

Mr. Chairman, while I am not in entire agreement with the suggested amendment, because I think it has faults, I think it is better than section 336 which is based on the arbitrary 150 per cent and the equally arbitrary 30,000 pound limit for cars. Arguments have been repeated. We have tried to show that conditions on which this section are founded are unfair and unsatisfactory, especially in the way they attempt to control the rates the railways can charge. We all feel that a railway, being a public business and in essence a monopoly, requires regulating. We also feel, as this bill tries to show, that railways ought to be allowed a legitimate profit. The problem arises in the use of the word "legitimate".
The minister told us carefully that the 150 per cent will not create hardship because it

will not affect the large bulk shipper. I wonder if his interpretation is correct. That figure, it is almost certain, will have an indirect effect on rates charged and on the negotiating of those rates between large bulk shippers and the railways. For that reason I do not believe that 150 per cent is a wise figure to select. But I find it difficult to determine what figure should be selected. Perhaps it would be better to eliminate the percentage and adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Springfield. This, of course, will entail difficulties, and undoubtedly there will be difficulty in regulating the figures he selects. The real problem is, what shall be the total permissive earnings? This has been considered in the past and a rough percentage has been used. We can use those, I think, when we try to set up total permissive earnings.
I think the last part of the amendment is wise; I do not think there is anything wrong with it at all. The provision-
-plus an amount computed as being the cost of capital applicable to the carriage of such goods.
-is logical and legitimate.
In the committee we tried to obtain information from the railway. We wanted to know what it considered should be the cost of capital. The railway has been as intractable in that regard as it has been in giving figures about its variable costs. As the railway has refused those figures, the committee found difficulty in arriving at a proper figure. As a committee we had not the power to insist on being given these figures. I doubt if it would have done serious harm to the railway, as the railway suggested, had we been given them.
I think the large shipper, the one who will negotiate with the railway, probably has a fair idea of what the costs of the railways are in moving his goods, and the railway has a fair idea of how much it can charge without eliminating the profit of the shipper completely. The railway knows it cannot charge more than the traffic will bear, but it can charge all that the traffic will bear. Under these circumstances it is better that we have this type of amendment which does not work on that basis. The 150 per cent figure will allow the railways to charge all that the traffic will bear.
As has been stated, there are large bulk shipments of up to 200,000 pounds, such as you have in the product industry, and the percentage figure becomes astronomical. The present section enables the traffic to be charged an exorbitant rate.

My question may be hypothetical but I can think of cases where the arithmetic is very real. Let us take the case of the potash producers in Saskatchewan or the people who ship sulphur to the west coast from Alberta. If they appeared before the commission and claimed that they were paying a disproportionately high contribution under their toll to capital and profit, because of the provision in the bill affecting this matter the transportation commission has the power to deal with it. They have the power to remedy it.
I am told that potash shippers at Esterhazy, Saskatchewan, are paying approximately $9 a ton from their shipping point to the seaport at Vancouver or wherever the product is loaded. The variable cost for the movement of grain from points in this area to Vancouver is around $3 or slightly less than $3 a ton for the same movement. Let us assume that the variable costs for moving potash and grain are approximately the same, because there is about the same weight per carload. It might be argued that the variable costs for moving grain are slightly higher than the costs for moving potash because of the differences in cars, and so on. Following up my assumption it appears that potash shippers are paying for variable costs plus 200 per cent.
I think it can be argued by the province of Saskatchewan that such a charge is prejudicial to the economy of that province and that the contribution above variable costs is unreasonable. If the figures will not be made available how is the province to make a case in defending its economy? Will it do what Manitoba did, hire cost analysts to do the job that the transportation commission has already done? This thinking holds true for shippers of sulphur in Alberta. Sulphur may be shipped by pipe line but it is not being so shipped now. If the province of Alberta is of the opinion that on this commodity too high a contribution is being paid to the railway, that too much is being paid toward capital and profits above variable costs, then I think it has a justifiable case because the province wants to see its sulphur industry expanding.
The minister will agree with me that any commodity, potash, sulphur or lumber, must get to market at competitive prices. That is vital to the economy of the area in which the industry is. The provinces, therefore, have a justifiable right to get the most favourable rate for shipping that is available.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PLACES OF CONFINEMENT
AMENDMENT RESPECTING PLACES OF CONFINEMENT
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-13, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
[The Chairman.]
He said: Admittedly, Mr. Speaker, this bill only tackles one of the many problems relating to our younger people and the relationship they have with the law. Last year an interdepartmental committee report, dealing with many other aspects of the situation, was made public. The bill before us is one that was prepared some time ago. If you look at its front page you will notice that we are now only four days from the anniversary of its first reading, and it was prepared long before then.
The Fauteux committee which examined certain penology matters more than ten years ago made a certain comment which is reprinted in the explanatory notes to this bill, and I think I would be unable to put things more succinctly than did Mr. Justice Fauteux in his report. I quote the following comment from page 27 of his report, as reproduced in the explanatory notes:
Young Offenders
It is an astonishing fact that under the present law in Canada, it is possible for a child under the age of sixteen to be convicted of a criminal offence in an adult court and be sentenced to a lengthy term of imprisonment in a penitentiary. This can happen in any of the many areas where the Juvenile Delinquents Act is not in force ... In our opinion legislative changes are needed immediately to provide that no person under the age of sixteen years shall be committed to penal institutions where adult prisoners are confined, and we recommend accordingly.
The force of that recommendation is underlined by reference to "immediately." That committee saw no reason why immediate action should not be taken.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
In 1956 this committee reported to the minister of justice. Though many recommendations of the Fauteux committee have gone by the board, and have in some cases been ignored by successive ministers of justice, it is a sad commentary on the government, on parliament, on sociologists and on anybody who has any real concern for the position of our younger people in our society that the report and recommendations of Mr. Justice Fauteux have been ignored for so long, when he himself said that legislative changes were needed immediately. They were needed in 1956, and before then.
The purpose of this bill is to put into legislative effect the recommendations of Mr. Justice Fauteux, that it will not be possible for a child to be committed or confined to a penitentiary where adults are imprisoned. No one will argue that it benefits younger people to be incarcerated in a penitentiary with
January 20, 19G7
hardened criminals who have committed crimes of all varieties and intensities. The general consensus throughout the nation, throughout the western world, is that it is undesirable to place younger persons in contact with people who have spent many years of their lives following the pursuits of crime, and in the penitentiaries. If for nothing else, penitentiaries are excellent places for an apprenticeship in crime. As I have said earlier, it is sad that this situation should prevail for such a long time without legislative action being taken about it.
We have had for some time the report of the committee on juvenile delinquency. I had postponed proceedings with respect to this bill since the committee made its report, hoping that the study which I thought the Solicitor General said would take place would reach a conclusion. I hoped that we should see the beneficial results of that study come to the fore in a legislative way in the relations with the various provinces. It seems that the study has not yet been completed, because we have not heard anything about it. It would appear that the study will not yield full or partial results during this year. There is no reference to action being taken on the report of the committee on juvenile delinquency in the legislative program which parliament has been asked to consider.
The report of the committee on juvenile delinquency is one of the most urgent problems confronting this nation. The Bank Act, which we are to deal with at some time in this session, is inconsequential when compared with the value that our younger people have in this society, and with the manner in which we treat them, and the things we do in disregard of their legitimate interests in this nation. The current bill before us, the transportation bill, vital through it is, is inconsequential when balanced against the needs of the younger people, and the need of this parliament to do something worth while with respect to young people who come in conflict with the law.
There is a crucial time in a person's life, the formative years, when society can help that individual. At that time society can help a younger person to overcome difficulties. That is the time when young people need help, because their paths either will lead to crime and successive years in penitentiaries, or down what we call the straight and narrow-in other words, into the main stream of social action. If we miss that crucial moment, all the successive attempts at rehabilitation

Juvenile Delinquents Act come to naught. The statistics on recidivism in our penitentiaries, the efforts which, with little effect, we make toward rehabilitation, the attempts we make at penological reform, whether in connection with the construction of institutions or practices within those institutions, show that there can be relatively little beneficial effect once a person becomes confirmed in his attitude toward society and toward the law.
That is why I say that, important as the transport bill may be to some, important as the Bank Act is, these are matters of no consequence when balanced against the value we should place on our young people, and the assistance we ought to give them at that crucial moment in their lives when they may overcome whatever psychological barriers or difficulties are confronting them.
This is why we have waited impatiently to hear what the government plans to do constructively with the extensive report of the committee on juvenile delinquency. I do not expect this bill will receive a fate different from that of other bills which have come up during this hour. In fact I feel it might be desirable if it were not given second reading, because the problem is much broader than this particular aspect of it. I hope however that at least we may be able to have a full round of comment about the general situation confronting our younger people, and their relationship with the law, as well as the application of law enforcement and penological methods. I hope the Solicitor General may say something with respect to the study taking place within his department about this important committee report.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have waited for some weeks to speak in the house during private members hour on this item of legislation. We should be thankful to the hon. member for Skeena for putting it on the order paper and for drawing this particular aspect of the problem of penology to our attention.
While I would support his bill heartily, let me say at the outset, as the hon. member said a few moments ago, that we are looking at just one aspect of a large problem. We are trying to straighten out what has become an increasingly bad social anomaly. If there is any area today in our country which has been kept very much in the dark and allowed to proceed at a slow rate of progress, in terms of our understanding of man, it is the area of what we do with social or criminal offenders.
January 20, 1967

Juvenile Delinquents Act [DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
I feel strongly, as does the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that by and large we have ignored all the new concepts which have come within our grasp during the last half century; we have made virtually no use of our new understanding of the best ways in which to deal with those who offend against our laws. Of course, I realize that we are dealing this evening with young people under the age of 16 who-though most people in Canada would find it hard to believe-are at this moment in prison side by side with some of the most hardened criminals who operate in this country. And this is done in the name of justice, or in the naive hope that we may be able to return to society young men who have somehow been chastened and reformed as a result of their experience. If there are those in this country today who are wondering where criminals are trained, developed and further motivated, they will find the major source not on the street corners or in the poolrooms, or in the shady lounges, but in institutions operated by federal and provincial governments -jails, prisons and penitentiaries.
I can speak about this from personal experience, for it was my duty during my student days in theology to work as a prison chaplain, to meet and talk with men in prison and watch some of them in their progress toward a full-time life of crime. I think a lot of nonsense has been written and produced on television screens to illustrate the ways in which people embark on a criminal way of life. From time to time we are told in lurid detail about people who come from good homes and who, because of some quirk, or unexplained desire, commit some act of crime. However interesting this may be, it is not a realistic picture.
At least 90 per cent of those who opt for a criminal way of life usually come from homes which are not very well organized, homes which are not strongly held together and which afford little support for an individual. In the beginning, very often, the crime is nothing more than a foolish act which led to a sentence of, perhaps, 30 days. It is during the serving of this first sentence that a life of crime is seriously contemplated.
I am sure that if one entered the great majority of county and provincial prisons this evening he would find young fellows barely old enough to shave, sitting on wooden benches talking to men of 45 and 50, men who have "been around," who know what the score is, who have discovered the short cuts and who have become habituated to a life of


crime punctuated by frequent sporadic terms of imprisonment. This is the situation which prevails not only in provincial prisons but in federal penitentiaries. Not only do we persist in causing relatively innocent offenders to associate with hardened three-time, six-time and ten-time losers, but we place them in an environment where it is almost impossible for them to avoid learning from their associates what further crimes might be perpetrated upon release. When we talk blandly about putting people behind bars to protect the rest of society, it is shocking to think that three out of every four of those who are presently behind bars will commit some further offence after their release, and be locked up once again.
I ask: What in God's name is the use of a system which affords almost no degree of protection for those who are free in society or to those who are now in prison and will at some point be released? We do all this in the name of justice. We have the extremely naive belief that through an arrangement of this kind men will be reformed, though it has been shown again and again in our era that hostility produces hostility, and that punishment produces reaction and violence. What do we gain by teaching young people in their teens that if they commit some anti-social act expressing their hostility to society, society will turn on the heat by exposing them to hostility exerted by social pressure?
This is why I say that in dealing with the bill sponsored by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) it would be folly on our part to ignore the wider problem which exists-the increasing pressure on our society because our prisons, as the figures tell us, are in most cases becoming increasingly occupied, our penitentiaries swollen to overflowing.
Yet we have not dealt with the nub of the problem. The nub of the problem is as old as our civilization itself. We are supposed to believe that when a person commits a criminal act in this ocuntry, the essential thing is that he must be punished. A good deal of the feeling which prevails in our country toward those who commit crimes was expressed during this session when we were discussing whether or not to abolish capital punishment. We did not take that opportunity. Speeches were made ad nauseam to the effect that we must always be sure we punish people who perpetrate crimes in our society. For what reason? Ought we to do this because it is our intention to teach them a lesson? Well, if three out of four people who enter prison
January 20, 1967	COMMONS
commit further crimes after their release, we have not taught them much of a lesson in my opinion. Is it because we intend to wreak a little vengeance upon them, just as might be done in private confrontations? If we feel that way, that is fine, but we should recognize that these people are being confined not for an altruistic reason, or in order to reform them, but simply because public vengeance must be taken. If this is the limit of our understanding of the problem, then all I can say is that I am sorry indeed for our society.
It was interesting to relate this attitude to the attitude of mind of our society 100 years ago toward the mentally deranged. Hon. members may have read in books or magazines that a mentally deranged person a hundred years ago was considered to be filled with an evil spirit, and it was thought that the best thing to do was to whip him, or otherwise torment him, in order that he should come to his senses. Hon. members may recall some of the horrible things which were done to people who were incurably insane in the name of medicine, and of good health.
Is this the level of understanding we have reached today when dealing with the mentally sick? It is not. When a person has a nervous breakdown or loses touch with reality, do we punish him? No; we are anxious to secure the best medical attention at the earliest moment so that, if at all possible, he can be restored to health. With the knowledge and expertise now available to us I hope we are coming quickly to the realization that in dealing with those who offend against society it is no longer enough to punish them or lock them away in some dark corner.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We must come to the realization that those who commit crimes are sick. They are not sick in the sense one is sick when a thermometer is put in his mouth and it is found that he has a high temperature. They are not sick in the sense that you can submit them to a questionnaire, and if they answer too many questions in a strange way you know their minds are not functioning properly. They are, however, sick in terms of not being able to live in a healthy way with the rest of society. This is a new kind of sickness which we must come to understand. It is a type of sickness which may start whith a young boy of six years of age when he decides that he wants to pick things off a shelf in a store because he wants something. Or it may be the type of sickness which develops in a man 55 years of age when he decides he can alter the ledger books in some
Juvenile Delinquents Act way and escape with thousands of dollars. Nonetheless, this is a sickness.
When we start to think in this enlightened way we will be able to do away with these damp, dark, infested holes that we call centres of justice and reform. We will be able to do away with these drab grey buildings which we think in some way protect society and reform the individual. I would hope that this bill would give us the opportunity to wrestle with this very deep social problem. I would hope that we would not run away from it and that we would not just tinker with it. I would hope we would use in an enlightened way the very best methods available to us today to help people who are socially sick, whether they be young or old. Then we might not have the situation in this country, as has been said again and again, where a young man who is 19 years of age is locked up for two years because he broke into a gas station, is let out again after 18 months, decides to steal a couple of cars, is locked up for another five years until he is 26 years of age, is let out again when he is 26, steals another car, and then is locked up again for nine years. This person's life at this stage has become a life of living like a common animal between four walls, and with bars on the windows.
This is not the type of life that was intended for any human being. It is not the life which was intended for you or me. I would hope that the government would take both this bill which is before us, and the thoughts I have expressed, under very serious consideration. In closing I might say I would hope that the penitentiary committee which was set up during this session, would become more active than it has been to date. Certainly very few meetings have been held since this session began, and now this session has gone on for 190 days. There does not seem to be any indication that they have taken this problem seriously.
I for one will look forward to a great deal of attention and a great deal of interest being given to this problem, because it stands as one of the greatest social problems which faces our country today.

speechtext:
The
social problem which is dealt with in Bill C-13 and the recommendation in respect of the repeal of subsection 2 of section 26 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act I am sure are topics which will appeal to all members of this house. All of us have a humanitarian interest in this. What shocks me greatly about this whole situation is the fact that there are many

January 20, 1967
Juvenile Delinquents Act fields in respect of which we impose laws governing youths of a certain age, but in what other fields do we have laws to protect our youth from certain aspects of our society? At the provincial level of government our laws provide for a curfew in certain cases, so that youths of a certain age must be off the street at a certain hour. We have laws which say that with some exceptions, they must attend school until they are 16 years of age. We have laws which state that youths cannot possess alcoholic beverages. They cannot purchase alcoholic beverages until they reach age 18 or age 21. They must be a certain age before they are entitled to hold a driver's licence. They must be a certain age before they can qualify for elective office. They must be a certain age before they are entitled to handle firearms.
We have not, however, placed a limit on the age at which they can be placed in a prison or other institution with adults who, as the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacDonald) has mentioned, are hardened criminals. I should like to compliment the hon. member for Prince for bringing out many of the social problems which are involved in dealing with these people in our modern society.
I think there are five major areas which should be considered when we discuss juvenile delinquency. One is the home. I am very much inclined to agree with the hon. member for Prince in this regard. I think that in these television programs the youths who become involved in crime in the first place are portrayed as being persons who have come from good homes. I believe the greatest enemy of our youth today possibly is poverty and the slum areas which exist in our cities across Canada. Where children are brought up in homes under responsible parents, and where there is an obvious communication between the parents and their children, one does not find that these children go very far astray.
I remember one particular case which arose during my teaching career. A young boy ran away from home. The father and mother did not seem to have any particular interest in locating him because they thought it would do him a lot of good to stay out all night, so that he would get hungry and perhaps want to come back home again. This was a case where there obviously was no communication.
Then there is the church in our society. I think this is a very important aspect, so far as juvenile delinquency is concerned, because every person in our society must have a certain faith, something to lean on in time of

trouble. Youths who are brought up in good homes usually are those who have attended church regularly, and they receive some excellent guidance there. At this point I should like to say that I have no respect for some of the television programs and some of the individuals who appear on television programs. Some of these people are agnostics who in our modern day society seem to think that it is important to knock religion on every possible occasion. When we knock religion and knock our traditions, we are knocking the base from under our society.
The third aspect is the school. Education is a very important factor. We must train our youth to play a useful role in society. I think our teachers could play a very important role in dealing with student problems by keeping in close contact with the home. The friends and associates, not just inside the prison walls, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, which the youth has in every-day society are very important to him. The youth can help those friends and associates, and they in turn can help him. Another important aspect is the society in which the youth lives. Advances in science and technology in the last few years have had a tremendous impact on our way of life. These advances have also had a great effect upon our humanitarian efforts.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
An hon. member mentioned that some laws which existed 100 years ago, both in England and here, were laws of persecution. No one in this house has a persecution complex, I am sure, but laws change more slowly than scientific approaches and technological understanding. My point is that when we adopt legislation of the kind now before us we should make sure that facilities and institutions are available to effectively take advantage of such legislation.
Like the hon. member for Prince, I want to compliment the hon. member who placed this bill before us. It always does us good to look seriously at situations and bring them to the attention of the individuals concerned. In support of the Solicitor General who has taken a great deal of interest in this matter, despite what some people may think, it was almost five years after the parliamentary committee studied juvenile delinquency before the report was tabled in the house. One should not be surprised that a final decision has not been made by the government.
Many conflicts of interest are involved in this matter of juvenile delinquency. Many aspects are outside the constitutional authority
January 20, 1967
of the federal government. During the past few years we have observed many examples of the difficulties involved in governing a country on a federal basis. Many things must be dealt with jointly by the federal and provincial governments. Before the recommendations of the report of that committee can be implemented a great deal of consultation will be required, and I may say that considerable consultation has already taken place. Many financial problems will have to be solved, including those in relation to financial assistance to provinces.
The report is divided basically into three parts. The first part deals with the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which is a federal statute; yet the administration of juvenile courts falls within provincial jurisdiction. The second part deals with federal-provincial relations. Part III deals with a research department which can be administered by either the federal or provincial governments. This presents another problem which must be solved. Plans and arrangements must be made so that programs dealing with juvenile delinquency and related prison reform can work effectively and efficiently in practice as well as in theory.
Let me quote from the final report of the Committee on Remission Service of 1956. This particular part is referred to in the bill now before us. I quote from page 27 of this report, which states in part:
It is an astonishing fact that under the present law in Canada, it is possible for a child under the age of sixteen to be convicted of a criminal offence in an adult court and be sentenced to a lengthy term of imprisonment in a penitentiary. This can happen in any of the many areas where the Juvenile Delinquents Act is not in force. Some provincial authorities have been authorized by the Prisons and Reformatories Act to make limited efforts to deal with this class of offender but the situation in Canada is, however, far from satisfactory.
The next paragraph indicates that in the year 1955, 14 persons under the age of 16 years were admitted to Canadian penitentiaries. Those 14 individuals are important to our society, and particularly important to other individuals of the same age group.
A very important paragraph of this report can be found at page 60, reading as follows:
A person who is sentenced to penitentiary does not begin to earn statutory remission until he arrives at the institution. Cases frequently occur where such persons are detained in the county jail so that they will be available as witnesses, or for some other reason, who will not earn remission while so detained.
Certain recommendations appear at page 87 of the report in respect of this very important
Juvenile Delinquents Act subject. I should like to quote several of these recommendations or goals to be achieved, and I will begin with (c) which refers to-
-a concentration of effort on treatment by way of training, rather than the near imposition of punishment; this is especially so in the case of special classes of offenders, particularly youthful offenders and persistent offenders;
Recommendation (d) sets forth as another goal the-
-specialization of institutions and specialization of methods of treatment, with a concentration of professional staff in the areas where it is most needed.
That is the very crux of this matter. We must employ sufficient number of specialists to work with these individuals so that these offenders do not continue to return to our prisons.
Another goal is set forth in (f) which calls for-
-a planned policy of recruitment and training of professional staff.
That is a necessary supplement to (d). The final goal or feature set out in this recommendation is (g) which asks for-
-a willingness to make full-scale experiments in all phases of the correctional system.
Let me turn to page 88 of this report and read several of the recommendations which appear there. I shall begin by reading No. 13 which states:
In any case where a convicted person is between the ages of 16 and 21 or where a maximum term of imprisonment of two years or more may he imposed, no offender should be sentenced to any term of imprisonment without consideration, by the court, of a pre-sentence report.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
Then No. 16 reads as follows:
Appropriate legislative amendments should be made immediately to provide that no person under the age of 16 years shall be committed to penal institutions where adult prisoners are confined.
Here I should like to refer back to something I said a few moments ago, namely that we make laws to keep out teenagers out of pool rooms, we make laws to keep our teenagers out of beverage rooms and other phases of our society, but we must implement a law that does not allow our people under the age of 16 years to associate, within the bounds of prison walls, with hardened criminals. Recommendation No. 20 reads as follows:
The federal and the provincial governments should give serious consideration, in expanding their systems of penal institutions, to the establishment, on a medium security basis, of such additional institutions as may be required.

Then No. 38:
Some means should be found to provide specialized after-care for particular types of parolees, such as sex offenders, drug addicts, alcoholics and psychopaths.
In my concluding remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to again pay tribute to the hon. member who brought this private bill before us and to the Solicitor General, who is in every sense a humanitarian individual, who is deeply interested in this matter and is doing a great deal of work in this regard. I know it will not be long before this problem is cured in our society. We cannot build schools to educate youth and at the same time have prisons which contain hardened criminals in which our youth are educated in a different direction from the way we want them educated in our society.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I would contend that the purpose of this bill is not an attack upon the Juvenile Delinquents Act. All it says is that the Juvenile Delinquents Act has a section in it which permits those charged under the Criminal Code to be removed from the protection of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. All this bill does is raise the age from 14 to 16 years, to give them this protection.
I doubt whether any member of parliament would deny the protection of the Juvenile Delinquents Act to a 16-year-old, rather than subjecting him to the mercy of the Criminal Code. I believe this is what we should be voting on in the next few minutes, and I do not think it should be the policy of the government to oppose this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why Bill No. C-13 does not deal with section 13 (3) of the Juvenile Delinquents Act, which is a pretty analogous section. Recently a case was argued before the Supreme Court of Canada. I believe this case was from the province of Alberta. It attacked the constitutional validity of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. I think the judgment in that case has been reserved. In that event it is probable that our Department of Justice, our Solicitor General and our Minister of Justice are somewhat embarrassed at the present time with respect to doing anything in the way of amending the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
As I understand it, in that case there was a minor, quasi-criminal offence committed-I believe it was under the Highway Traffic Act-and a charge was laid under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, a federal statute, instead of by way of summary conviction. This is what started the whole question of whether the Juvenile Delinquents Act was ultra vires. A great problem is posed at the present time for our ministry in this connection. The report of the Department of Justice, which has been so much referred to, was brought down in the year 1965, I believe, but was not tabled until February, 1966. I see here the library filing mark which says "February 22, 1966." I understand that report took about five years to prepare; therefore hon. members will understand that a great deal is involved in this question.
The aim of Bill No. C-13 is to ensure that no child who has committed an offence shall, upon conviction, be confined in a place of imprisonment for adults. Of course no one disagrees with that. This section does not apply to a child who has been proceeded against under the provisions of section 9.
